Wilson Disease

copper and ATP7B · liver plus brain, eye or red cells · ceruloplasmin, slit lamp, urine copper · chelation or transplantDoes unexplained liver disease come with brain, eye or red-cell findings, and is the ceruloplasmin low?

Source vignette Pt – teen whose hepatitis may be advancing toward cirrhosis, now with tremor, slurred speech and a change in behavior · Exam – golden-brown rings at the rim of the cornea · Labs – raised transaminases · Q – which mechanism underlies the disease

1Illness script
Bottom line
  • Screen for Wilson disease in unexplained liver disease under 40, above all with tremor, dysarthria or psychiatric change, Kayser-Fleischer rings or Coombs-negative hemolysis.
  • Screen with serum ceruloplasmin (low) plus a slit-lamp exam; confirm with a high 24-hour urine copper, and let liver biopsy copper settle tests that disagree.
  • Treat for life: a chelator (penicillamine or trientine), then zinc or a lower dose for maintenance; fulminant liver failure needs a liver transplant.
What it is

Wilson disease (hepatolenticular degeneration): autosomal recessive copper overload of the liver, then the brain, cornea, red cells and kidneys.

Driver

Loss of ATP7B (chromosome 13), the hepatocyte copper pump; its relative, copper-transporting ATPase 7A (ATP7A), causes Menkes disease.

Triggers

Copper builds from birth, so none is needed. A sibling, parent or cousin with the disease

non-modifiable

; age under 40, with symptoms usually from 5 to 35

non-modifiable

Chain

ATP7B fails in the hepatocyte

copper is neither excreted into bile nor loaded onto ceruloplasmin, so ceruloplasmin falls

copper accumulates in the liver: hepatitis, then fibrosis and cirrhosis

free copper spills into the blood

it deposits in the basal ganglia, the Descemet membrane of the cornea, red cells and the renal tubule

movement and psychiatric signs, Kayser-Fleischer rings, hemolysis, Fanconi syndrome

Insights

Ceruloplasmin is an acute phase reactant, so active hepatitis can lift it to normal; carriers and other liver diseases can also run low, so one borderline value does not decide it.

Total serum copper usually runs low because most of it rides on ceruloplasmin, while free copper runs high and does the damage in the brain, cornea and red cells.

Birthcopper starts to build in the liver
Childhood and adolescencehepatitis is the first sign in almost half: acute, chronic or fulminant
Young adultsneurologic or psychiatric onset in about 40%
Untreatedfatal, usually by age 30
2Urgent risks
Act now
FindingAction
Jaundice and confusion with a high international normalized ratio (INR) and Coombs-negative hemolysis in a teen or young adultFulminant Wilson disease: liver transplant may be lifesaving, so refer now (step 7).
New psychosis or a movement disorder with ataxia, dysarthria or abnormal liver testsAdd serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urine copper to the workup.
A treated patient plans to stop medicationDo not stop: stopping can bring on acute liver failure (step 8).
3Differential
Unexplained liver disease, young patient
DiagnosisDecides itNext best step
Autoimmune hepatitisYoung woman, often with another autoimmune disease; no neurologic signs or corneal rings.Antinuclear antibody (ANA), anti-smooth muscle antibody (in children, anti-liver kidney microsomal type 1 antibody) and immunoglobulin G; check ceruloplasmin too, since Wilson disease can mimic it.
Viral hepatitisThe most common cause: exposure risk for hepatitis B or C, or an acute hepatitis A illness; no neurologic signs, rings or hemolysis.Order A, B and C serologies.
Hereditary hemochromatosisAutosomal recessive iron overload that presents after 40: diabetes, bronze skin, arthropathy; iron does not cause tremor or corneal rings.Check transferrin saturation and ferritin.
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiencyHepatocytes retain a misfolded protein: cholestasis in newborns, cirrhosis in adults, early basal emphysema; the lung, not the brain or eye, is its second organ.Measure its serum level.
MASLD (metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease) Obesity, diabetes, dyslipidemia, a mild ALT-predominant rise and a bright liver on ultrasound; nothing outside the liver.Diagnose it by exclusion after testing for the other causes.
Antipsychotic-induced parkinsonism Tremor, rigidity or dystonia that follows a dopamine blocker; liver tests normal, so it does not explain liver disease.Match the onset to the drug start.
4Workup
Clues that change the answer
CluePoints toNext best step
Golden-brown ring at the corneal marginKayser-Fleischer ring: copper in the Descemet membraneOrder serum ceruloplasmin and 24-hour urine copper
Tremor, slurred speech or falling grades in a teen with hepatitisNeurologic Wilson diseaseOrder a slit-lamp exam; rings are almost always present
Normal ceruloplasmin during active hepatitisA false normal from the acute phase riseSend a 24-hour urine copper

Pause point. A normal ceruloplasmin in active hepatitis does not end the search: the urine copper or the liver biopsy decides.

5Diagnostic criteria
Rules
ResultMeans
Low ceruloplasmin plus a Kayser-Fleischer ringDiagnostic
Low ceruloplasmin plus high 24-hour urine copperDiagnosis clear
Rings plus typical motor signsNearly pathognomonic
Ceruloplasmin under 5 mg/dLHighly suggestive, whatever the clinical picture
Indeterminate tests and no ringsLiver biopsy for hepatic copper
6Severity
Presentation and what it means
FindingMeaning
Raised transaminases without symptomsEarly disease
CirrhosisTreated with a chelator; transplant for severe liver failure despite drugs (step 7); adds hepatocellular carcinoma risk
Neurologic or psychiatric signsCopper has left the liver; Kayser-Fleischer rings almost always present
Acute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolysisFulminant disease: liver transplant (step 7)
7Treatment
1

SymptomaticHepatic or neurologic disease

First line: a chelator, penicillamine (most used) or trientine (the alternative; penicillamine is more likely to cause side effects), plus a low-copper diet. Fever, rash, low neutrophils and platelets, proteinuria and membranous nephropathy (membranous glomerulonephritis); pyridoxine is given with it, and neurologic signs can worsen when chelation starts.

2

MaintenanceCopper removed and symptoms improved

Lower-dose chelator or oral zinc, which reduces gut copper absorption; zinc is not given at the same time as a chelator.

3

PresymptomaticRelative found by screening, no symptoms

Zinc for a presymptomatic relative.

4

Chelator failsChelator not tolerated, or neurologic signs not responding

Zinc acetate as the alternative.

5

Liver failureAcute (fulminant) liver failure, or severe liver failure despite drugs

Liver transplant, which cures the disease in most cases.

8Follow-up
After diagnosis
SituationDo
Every patientLifelong therapy, with or without symptoms; stopping can bring on acute liver failure.
On treatmentFollow 24-hour urine copper; penicillamine is dosed to urine copper and free serum copper.
Sibling, parent or cousinScreen: slit-lamp exam, liver tests, ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urine copper and, if available, ATP7B testing.
Infant relativeTest after age 1 year; ceruloplasmin is low in the first months of life.
PregnancyContinue treatment throughout.
Practice
  1. 16 yo M with several months of fatigue and mild jaundice, a new hand tremor, slurred speech and irritability with falling grades; elevated AST and ALT; golden-brown rings at the corneal margins on slit-lamp exam → Defective copper transport in hepatocytes → Wilson disease: ATP7B failure blocks biliary copper excretion and copper loading onto ceruloplasmin, so copper deposits in the liver, basal ganglia and cornea
  2. 19 yo F with 3 months of fatigue and a fine hand tremor; ALT 240, AST 190, bilirubin normal; hepatitis B and C serologies negative; ferritin and transferrin saturation normal; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody negative; normal body mass index and no alcohol use → Serum ceruloplasmin → screen for Wilson disease in a young patient with unexplained hepatitis and a tremor; slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper follow
  3. 17 yo F with Hashimoto thyroiditis and 6 weeks of fatigue, joint aches and jaundice; ALT 850, AST 700; serum IgG high; ANA and anti-smooth muscle antibody positive; ceruloplasmin normal; no Kayser-Fleischer rings; normal neurologic exam → Autoimmune hepatitis → corticosteroids, with azathioprine to spare steroids
  4. 21 yo M with 1 year of hand tremor and dysarthria; compensated cirrhosis on imaging, INR 1.3, no ascites or encephalopathy; ceruloplasmin low, 24-hour urine copper high, Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam → Oral penicillamine → symptomatic Wilson disease: lifelong chelation (penicillamine or trientine), zinc later for maintenance
  5. 18 yo F with 1 week of jaundice, now confused; INR 3.2; hemoglobin 7.8 with high reticulocytes and a negative direct Coombs test; Kayser-Fleischer rings on slit-lamp exam; no acetaminophen ingestion → Urgent liver transplantation → fulminant Wilson disease: acute liver failure with Coombs-negative hemolysis does not recover with chelation alone
  6. 14 yo M, asymptomatic, whose 17-year-old sister was just diagnosed with Wilson disease; normal growth and development; normal physical and neurologic exam → Serum ceruloplasmin and liver tests → siblings carry a 1 in 4 risk; add a slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper, and treat presymptomatic disease with zinc
  7. 24 yo M with Wilson disease treated with penicillamine for 3 years; tremor resolved, liver tests now normal, urine copper at target; asks about coming off medication → Stopping copper-lowering therapy → treatment is lifelong; stopping can precipitate acute liver failure
Management Symptomatic disease: copper chelation with penicillamine or trientine, lifelong, with a low-copper diet (avoid shellfish, organ meats, nuts, chocolate and mushrooms) · Maintenance or presymptomatic disease: zinc, which reduces intestinal copper absorption · Fulminant liver failure: urgent liver transplantation, which corrects the liver defect · Family: screen first-degree relatives, siblings above all (a 1 in 4 chance of disease, since it is autosomal recessive), with ceruloplasmin, liver tests, a slit-lamp exam and 24-hour urine copper · Never stop: stopping therapy can precipitate acute liver failure
Pearls Psychiatric change or falling school performance can precede the liver findings. A young patient with new psychiatric illness and abnormal liver tests needs a ceruloplasmin · Acute liver failure with a Coombs-negative hemolytic anemia in a teen or young adult is fulminant Wilson disease. It needs a transplant center, not chelation alone · A presumed autoimmune hepatitis in a young patient should have ceruloplasmin checked before steroids · Serum total copper is usually low; urine copper is high
Pairs with Fatty Liver Disease lists Wilson disease among the exclusions: is there tremor or Kayser-Fleischer rings, and is the ceruloplasmin low? Abnormal Liver Tests places Wilson in the hepatocellular pattern: are the transaminases, not the alkaline phosphatase, leading? Hemolytic Anemia covers the other Coombs-negative hemolysis of the young: are there spherocytes and an affected parent, or liver disease with corneal rings? Tick-Borne Illness holds the acute mimic: did confusion with transaminitis arrive over hours with fever and a rash, or over months with a tremor?
Transferable rule When unexplained liver disease comes with a finding outside the liver, identify the organ. Brain, cornea or red cells point to copper, and the lung points to alpha-1 antitrypsin. The pancreas, skin, joints and heart in an older patient point to iron.
Class-vs-memberIncreased intestinal iron absorption: the right class, an inherited metal overload of the liver, but the wrong metal; HFE hemochromatosis presents in middle age with diabetes, skin and joint findings, never tremor or corneal rings.
Unchecked attributeHepatocyte retention of a misfolded protease inhibitor: alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency is an inherited liver disease of the young, but its second organ is the lung; it does not explain neuropsychiatric signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings.
